nodes.name: Hiranyakashipu
nodes.description: The mighty Daitya king, eldest son of the sage Kashyapa and Diti, and so a half-brother of the Adityas. Empowered by a near-perfect boon from Brahma, he conquered the three worlds and persecuted his own son Prahlada for worshipping Vishnu, until Vishnu appeared as Narasimha to slay him.
nodes.story: After Varaha slew his brother Hiranyaksha, Hiranyakashipu swore vengeance on Vishnu and practised austerities on Mount Mandara so fierce that ants built a mound over his body. Brahma granted him a boon: he could be killed by no being Brahma had created, neither man nor beast, neither by day nor by night, neither indoors nor outdoors, neither on the ground nor in the sky, by no weapon. He conquered the three worlds and banned the worship of Vishnu, yet his son Prahlada stayed devoted through poison, elephants, serpents and fire. Mocking the boy, the king struck a pillar and asked whether his Vishnu lived there too. Narasimha, neither man nor lion, burst from it at twilight, seized him at the threshold, laid him across his lap and tore him open with his claws, honouring every clause of the boon.
nodes.abode: Hiranyapura, the golden city of the Daityas
variations: In the Vishnu Purana the story centres on Prahlada's sufferings and the slaying is told briefly; the Bhagavata Purana gives the full boon and the pillar scene.
The Bhagavata Purana (Cantos 3 and 7) and Vishnu Purana 4.15 treat him as the first of three births of Vishnu's cursed doorkeepers, followed by Ravana and Shishupala.
Texts differ on which twin was elder: the Bhagavata calls Hiranyakashipu the elder, while other tellings make Hiranyaksha the first conceived.

nodes.name: Hiranyaksha
nodes.description: The 'golden-eyed' Daitya, son of Kashyapa and Diti and twin brother of Hiranyakashipu. A restless warrior who sought an equal in battle, he was slain by Vishnu in his boar avatar, Varaha, while the Earth was being raised from the cosmic ocean.
nodes.story: The twins were born of Diti's union with Kashyapa at the inauspicious hour of dusk, and the worlds shook with portents at their birth. Hiranyaksha grew into a giant who roamed the three worlds with his mace, looking for anyone who would fight him; the devas hid, and he lashed the waves of the ocean for sport. He challenged Varuna, lord of the waters, who told him that only Vishnu was his match. So Hiranyaksha found Vishnu in the form of the boar Varaha, lifting the Earth from the depths on his tusks. The asura jeered and attacked, hurling mace, trident and conjured illusions, and the duel shook the cosmos. At last Varaha struck him beneath the ear with his hand, and Hiranyaksha fell, his face shining as he gazed upon the Lord who freed him.
nodes.abode: Rasatala and the depths of the cosmic ocean
variations: In early Varaha accounts (Brahmanas, Vishnu Purana) the boar simply raises the sunken Earth; the duel with Hiranyaksha is a Puranic addition.
Many later and popular tellings say Hiranyaksha himself dragged the Earth down into the ocean; in the Bhagavata it had sunk and he meets Varaha during the rescue.
In the Shiva and Linga Puranas Shiva gives the childless Hiranyaksha the blind boy Andhaka as his son.

nodes.name: Prahlada
nodes.description: Son of Hiranyakashipu and Kayadhu, Prahlada is revered as one of the greatest devotees (bhaktas) of Vishnu. Though born a Daitya prince, his unshakable faith through his father's persecution made him the model of devotion; he later ruled the Daityas justly and was grandfather of Bali.
nodes.story: While still in his mother's womb, Prahlada absorbed the sage Narada's teachings on devotion. As a boy he was sent to be schooled by Shanda and Amarka, sons of Shukracharya, but instead he taught his classmates to love Vishnu. Enraged, Hiranyakashipu tried to kill him: poison, trampling elephants, venomous serpents, a fall from a cliff and a blazing fire, yet each time Prahlada remained unhurt, absorbed in the Lord. Asked where his Vishnu was, he replied that the Lord is everywhere, even in the pillar before them. When Narasimha burst forth and slew his father, even the gods feared the man-lion's fury; only the child approached and calmed him with hymns. Offered any boon, Prahlada asked only that his father be purified and that he himself never desire anything in return for devotion.
nodes.abode: Hiranyapura; later Sutala with his grandson Bali
sources: Taittiriya Brahmana (as Prahrada Kayadhava, an asura)
Mahabharata, Shanti Parva 124 (Prahlada gives away his shila)
variations: In the Taittiriya Brahmana Prahrada Kayadhava is simply an asura; his identity as the great devotee of Vishnu is epic and Puranic.
In the Mahabharata he is a wise and righteous asura king who teaches dharma and honestly judges against his own son Virochana.
The Vamana Purana tells of his battle with, and then devotion to, Nara-Narayana at Badari, and of his curse on Bali for slighting Vishnu.
Folk tradition in North India links him to Holika Dahan, where the fire burns Holika but spares him.

nodes.name: Kayadhu
nodes.description: Queen of Hiranyakashipu and mother of Prahlada, described in the Bhagavata Purana as a daughter of the Danava Jambha. While pregnant she lived in the hermitage of Narada, whose teaching shaped her unborn son.
nodes.story: While Hiranyakashipu was away performing his long austerities, Indra and the devas raided the Daitya capital. Indra seized the pregnant Kayadhu, meaning to destroy the child in her womb before another great asura could be born. The sage Narada stopped him on the road, declaring that the unborn child was a great devotee of Vishnu who could never be harmed. Indra released her, and Narada took Kayadhu to his hermitage, where she served him devotedly until her husband returned. There Narada taught her about dharma, the nature of the self and love for Vishnu. The Bhagavata says that Kayadhu in time forgot the teaching, but the child listening in her womb remembered every word. That child was born as Prahlada, a devotee from before his birth.
nodes.abode: Hiranyapura; Narada's hermitage during her pregnancy
sources: Taittiriya Brahmana (implied by the matronymic Kayadhava)
variations: The Vedic record knows her only through her son's matronymic 'Kayadhava'; her story is Puranic.
Some regional retellings call Prahlada's mother Leelavati rather than Kayadhu.

nodes.name: Virochana
nodes.description: Son of Prahlada and father of Bali, Virochana was a king of the asuras. He is best known from the Chandogya Upanishad, where he and Indra study the nature of the Self under Prajapati, and Virochana goes away believing the body is the Self.
nodes.story: Hearing that Prajapati taught of a Self free from sin, old age, death, grief, hunger and thirst, Indra of the devas and Virochana of the asuras each came to him as students. After thirty-two years of discipline, Prajapati told them to look at themselves in a pan of water, finely dressed and adorned, and said that what they saw was the Self. Virochana went away content and taught the asuras that the body is the Self, to be adorned, fed and served; the Upanishad says that is why the dead are decked with clothes and ornaments. Indra, however, grew uneasy on the road, returned, and after many more years of study learned that the true Self is not the body at all. In the Mahabharata, Virochana later contests with the brahmin Sudhanvan, and his father Prahlada rules against him.
symbols: mirror or pan of water (Chandogya episode)
variations: Some Puranic and folk tellings make Virochana so generous that he gave up his own life or crown to Indra disguised as a brahmin; this is not in the Upanishad.
In the Mahabharata's dispute over precedence with Sudhanvan, Prahlada's honest verdict against his son is praised as a model of truthfulness.

nodes.name: Mahabali
nodes.description: The generous and righteous Daitya emperor, son of Virochana and grandson of Prahlada, who ruled the three worlds until Vishnu as the dwarf Vamana asked him for three paces of land. Honoured for keeping his word and for his devotion, he was granted the netherworld Sutala and is remembered in Kerala during Onam as a beloved king whose reign was a golden age.
nodes.story: Guided by his guru Shukracharya, Bali conquered heaven and ruled the three worlds. To restore the devas, Vishnu was born to Aditi and Kashyapa as the dwarf Vamana, who came to Bali's great sacrifice and asked for just three paces of land. Shukracharya warned that the boy was Vishnu himself, but Bali would not break a promise to a brahmin, and his angry guru cursed him to lose his fortune. As Bali poured the water of the gift, Vamana grew into Trivikrama, spanning the earth with one stride and the heavens with the second. With no place left for the third, Bali humbly offered his own head. Pleased by his truthfulness and surrender, Vishnu gave him the realm of Sutala, promised to stand guard at his door, and named him Indra of a future age.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda (Siddhashrama and Vamana)
variations: The Bhagavata Purana makes him Indra of the eighth Manvantara (Savarni) and has Vishnu guard his gate in Sutala.
In Kerala's Onam tradition Mahabali (Maveli) was a just king under whom all people were equal, and he returns each year to visit his people.
The Vamana Purana adds that Prahlada cursed Bali to lose his kingdom for speaking slightingly of Vishnu.
Some tellings say Vamana pushed Bali down to Patala with his foot; others stress that Bali went to Sutala honoured, not destroyed.

nodes.name: Banasura
nodes.description: The thousand-armed asura king of Shonitapura, eldest of Bali's hundred sons and a great devotee of Shiva. His daughter Usha's love for Aniruddha, Krishna's grandson, led to a war in which Shiva fought on Bana's side against Krishna.
nodes.story: Bana pleased Shiva by playing drums with his thousand arms during the god's dance, and Shiva agreed to guard his city of Shonitapura. Proud and restless, Bana complained that his arms itched for a worthy fight; Shiva said he would find one when his banner fell. Bana's daughter Usha dreamed of a handsome prince, and her friend Chitralekha, recognising Aniruddha from her portraits, carried him by magic from Dvaraka into Usha's chamber. Discovering the lovers, Bana bound Aniruddha with serpent-nooses. Krishna, Balarama and Pradyumna marched on the city; Shiva, Kartikeya and Shiva's fever-weapon fought for Bana. Krishna severed all but four of Bana's arms with his discus, but spared his life when Shiva interceded for his devotee. Bana bowed, Usha married Aniruddha, and Bana became one of Shiva's attendants.
weapons: bows and arrows in a thousand hands
variations: Shonitapura is located by tradition in Assam (Tezpur), in the Himalaya, or elsewhere; regional claims differ.
In the Shiva Purana Bana ends as Mahakala, a chief of Shiva's ganas.
In the separate South Indian legend of Kanyakumari, a demon Banasura is slain by the virgin goddess Kanya Kumari.

nodes.name: Holika
nodes.description: Sister of Hiranyakashipu, who was immune to fire and tried to burn the boy Prahlada on a pyre. The fire consumed her instead, and the bonfire of Holika Dahan on the eve of Holi commemorates the victory of devotion over malice.
nodes.story: When poison, elephants and serpents had all failed to kill Prahlada, Hiranyakashipu turned to his sister Holika, who could not be harmed by fire. She took the boy onto her lap and sat in the middle of a great pyre while the Daitya's servants lit it. Prahlada did not struggle; he simply kept repeating the name of Vishnu. The flames rose, and to the court's astonishment it was Holika who burned to ashes while the child emerged untouched. In some tellings her protection came from a fire-proof shawl that the wind lifted from her shoulders and wrapped around Prahlada; in others her immunity failed because she used a divine gift to harm an innocent. Across India bonfires are lit on the night before Holi to recall her burning.
sources: Popular Holi tradition of North India
Late Puranic and mahatmya literature on Holi
Bhavishya Purana, Uttara Parva (parallel Holi legend of the demoness Dhundha)
variations: The source of her immunity varies: a boon (often said to be from Brahma), or a shawl or cloth that could not burn.
The Bhavishya Purana gives a different origin of the Holi bonfire, the burning away of the demoness Dhundha who troubled children.
Holika is absent from the Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas, which list fire among Prahlada's ordeals without naming her.

nodes.name: Vritra
nodes.description: The great serpent-dragon of the Rig Veda who held back the waters by coiling around the mountains, and whom Indra slew with the vajra, releasing the rivers. Son of Danu in the Veda, he becomes Tvashtr's son in later texts, and the Bhagavata Purana portrays him as a profound devotee of Vishnu.
nodes.story: The Rig Veda sings how the serpent Vritra lay upon the mountain, holding the waters captive. Indra, strengthened by soma from three bowls, took up the thunderbolt that Tvashtr had fashioned and struck the first-born of serpents, splitting him apart. The released waters rushed down to the sea like lowing cows, and the sun, sky and dawn were set free. When Vritra's mother Danu tried to shield him, Indra struck her too, and she fell like a cow beside her calf. Later tellings add that Tvashtr created Vritra to avenge his son Vishvarupa, that Vritra swallowed Indra, and that the gods forged a new vajra from the bones of the sage Dadhichi. In the Bhagavata, before the final duel, Vritra prays to Vishnu and meets death gladly as liberation.
sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva and Udyoga Parva
variations: In the Rig Veda Vritra is son of Danu, a Danava; in the Brahmanas and Puranas he arises from Tvashtr's sacrifice to avenge Vishvarupa.
The Bhagavata Purana (6.14-17) says Vritra was the Vidyadhara king Chitraketu in a former life, reborn as an asura through Parvati's curse.
The Mahabharata (Udyoga Parva) tells of a truce under which Vritra could be slain neither by day nor night, wet nor dry; Indra killed him at twilight with sea-foam into which Vishnu had entered.
The myth has close Indo-Iranian parallels, such as Verethragna, 'smiter of resistance', in the Avesta.

nodes.name: Vishvarupa (Trishiras)
nodes.description: The three-headed son of the divine artisan Tvashtr, whose mother was of asura descent. In the Rig Veda he is slain by Trita Aptya and Indra; in later texts he serves as priest of the devas while secretly favouring the asuras, and his killing by Indra brings on Indra the sin of slaying a brahmin and provokes the creation of Vritra.
nodes.story: Vishvarupa had three heads: with one he drank soma, with another sura, and with the third he ate food. When Brihaspati withdrew from the gods, they chose this learned son of Tvashtr as their priest, and he taught Indra the protective Narayana Kavacha. Yet his mother came from the asuras, and during the sacrifices he quietly passed a share of the offerings to them. Discovering this, Indra struck off all three heads, which flew away as birds: the francolin, the sparrow and the partridge. Because Vishvarupa was a brahmin, Indra bore the stain of brahmin-slaying and shared it out among the earth, the waters, the trees and women. Grief-stricken, Tvashtr poured an oblation into the fire to raise up an enemy for Indra, and from it rose the great Vritra.
variations: In Rig Veda 10.8 it is Trita Aptya, sent by Indra, who slays the three-headed son of Tvashtr and frees his cows; Indra cuts off the heads.
In the Mahabharata Trishiras is an ascetic whose austerities threaten Indra; Indra's vajra kills him and a woodcutter severs the heads.
The Bhagavata names his mother Rachana, of Daitya birth, explaining his secret loyalty to the asuras.

nodes.name: Namuchi
aliases: the Danava who would not let go
nodes.description: A Danava of the Rig Veda whom Indra slew by beheading him with the foam of the waters. Later texts tell of a pact of friendship that forbade Indra from killing him by day or night, with anything wet or dry, a story at the heart of the Sautramani rite.
nodes.story: Indra and Namuchi swore friendship, and Indra promised never to slay him by day or by night, with anything wet or dry, with staff or bow, with palm or fist. Namuchi then made Indra drunk with sura and drained him of his strength, his soma and his vigour. Weakened and ashamed, Indra turned to the Ashvins and Sarasvati, who restored him, and together they found a way around the oath. At dawn, when it was neither day nor night, Indra took the foam of the waters, which is neither wet nor dry, and with it twisted off Namuchi's head. The Shatapatha Brahmana says the severed head rolled after Indra crying out that he was a betrayer of his friend. The Sautramani sacrifice, with its offerings of sura, re-enacts Indra's healing after this struggle.
variations: In the Mahabharata's Shalya Parva the severed head pursues Indra until he bathes at the confluence of the Aruna and Sarasvati.
In the Bhagavata Purana Namuchi fights in the war after the churning of the ocean, and Indra kills him with foam after the vajra fails.
Epic genealogies list Namuchi among the sons of Danu and Kashyapa.

nodes.name: Shambara
nodes.description: In the Rig Veda, a lord of mountain fortresses and foe of King Divodasa, whose ninety-nine forts Indra shattered. In the epics and Puranas, Shambara is a Danava of great sorcery who abducted the infant Pradyumna and was slain by him when he grew up.
nodes.story: Warned that Krishna's son would one day kill him, the Danava Shambara stole the infant Pradyumna from the birthing chamber in Dvaraka and threw him into the sea. A great fish swallowed the child, fishermen caught it, and the fish was brought to Shambara's own kitchen. When it was cut open, the baby was given to the kitchen's mistress, Mayavati, who was in truth Rati, the wife of Kama, waiting for her husband's rebirth. She raised Pradyumna and, when he came of age, revealed who he was and taught him the great art of illusion. Pradyumna challenged Shambara, countered every illusion the sorcerer hurled, and cut off his head. He then returned to Dvaraka with Mayavati, and Rukmini recognised her lost son.
nodes.abode: Ninety-nine (or a hundred) mountain forts (Rig Veda); his city by the sea (Puranas)
variations: The Rig Veda says Indra found Shambara dwelling in the mountains in the fortieth autumn and hurled him down, destroying his forts for Divodasa Atithigva.
Whether the Vedic chieftain-demon and the Puranic sorcerer are the same figure is debated; they share only the name.
Epic genealogies list Shambara among the sons of Danu; the Bhagavata also names a Shambara among Hiranyaksha's sons.

nodes.name: Vala
nodes.description: In the Rig Veda, Vala ('enclosure') is the rock cave, personified as a demon, in which the cattle of light were hidden by the Panis. Indra and Brihaspati, with the singing Angirases, broke it open and released the cows, the dawns and the sun.
nodes.story: The Panis had stolen the cows and hidden them deep inside the rock called Vala. Indra sent his dog Sarama across the far river to track them; she found the cattle and refused the Panis' bribes to betray the gods. Then Brihaspati, lord of sacred speech, came with the Angiras seers, and they sang. At the sound of the chant the rock split open like an egg, Indra broke through Vala's walls with his might, and the lowing cows streamed out into the light. With them came the dawns and the sun, which had been shut up in the darkness. Priests re-enacted this opening in the morning sacrifice, and Indra came to be praised as Valabhid, the breaker of Vala.
nodes.abode: A rock cave or mountain beyond the river Rasa
variations: Vala is sometimes a place or obstacle and sometimes a demon; scholars read the myth as the release of light, rain or poetic insight.
In later texts the name becomes Bala, a Danava slain by Indra; the Bhagavata Purana (5.24) makes Bala a son of Maya who lives in Atala.
Some hymns credit Brihaspati, others Indra, and others the Angirases' song with breaking the rock.

nodes.name: Puloman
nodes.description: A Danava, son of Kashyapa and Danu, and father of Shachi (Paulomi), the queen of Indra. Later texts say Indra slew him, earning the epithet Pulomajit, the conqueror of Puloman.
nodes.story: Shachi, the most beautiful of the Danava daughters, was the child of Puloman, and Indra chose her as his queen. Later tellings say that Puloman opposed the match, and that Indra killed his own father-in-law, which is why poets call Indra Pulomajit and Pulomari, conqueror and foe of Puloman. The Mahabharata's opening books tell a different tale of a being with the same name: a rakshasa Puloman had been promised the maiden Puloma before her father gave her to the sage Bhrigu. When Bhrigu was away, the rakshasa asked the sacred fire whose wife she was, and Agni reluctantly told the truth. Puloman took the form of a boar and carried her off, but her unborn child slipped from her womb, blazing like the sun, and reduced the abductor to ashes. The child was named Chyavana, 'the fallen one'.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (lists of the Danavas)
variations: The rakshasa Puloman who abducts Bhrigu's wife in the Mahabharata may be a separate figure from the Danava father of Shachi.
Indra's slaying of Puloman is known mainly from epithets (Pulomajit, Pulomari) and later tellings rather than a detailed early narrative.

nodes.name: Shukracharya (Ushanas Kavya)
nodes.description: A great Bhargava sage, son of Bhrigu, who became the guru of the asuras and the master of the Mrita Sanjivani, the knowledge that restores the dead. He is also Shukra, the planet Venus among the Navagraha, and the father of Devayani; his treatise on polity (Shukraniti) is attributed to him.
nodes.story: The devas could not match the asuras while Shukracharya kept reviving their fallen warriors, so Brihaspati's son Kacha came to him as a student, hoping to learn the Sanjivani. Shukra's daughter Devayani fell in love with the youth. The jealous asuras killed Kacha again and again, and each time Devayani begged her father to revive him. At last they burned him, mixed his ashes in wine and gave it to Shukra to drink. When Kacha answered his guru's call from inside his belly, Shukra saw that he could save his pupil only by dying himself. So he taught Kacha the Sanjivani there and then; Kacha burst out and revived his teacher. Horrified at what drink had led him to, Shukra declared that any brahmin who drank liquor would fall from his station.
nodes.vahana: Chariot drawn by eight horses (as the planet Shukra)
nodes.abode: The court of the asura kings; as a graha, the heavens
variations: In the Rig Veda, Kavya Ushanas is an ancient sage who helps Indra and fashions his vajra; his role as guru of the asuras is epic and Puranic.
The Mahabharata (Shanti Parva) tells that Shiva swallowed him and released him through his body, whence the name Shukra ('semen', 'bright').
Some Puranas say he received the Sanjivani from Shiva after severe austerities; others say he lost an eye when Vamana pierced the spout of Bali's water-pot, in which he had hidden.
The Matsya and Padma Puranas say Vishnu beheaded Shukra's mother for sheltering the asuras, and Bhrigu cursed Vishnu to be born repeatedly on earth.

nodes.name: Mayasura
nodes.description: The great architect and master of illusion among the Danavas, counterpart to the devas' Vishvakarma. He built the golden cave-city of the Ramayana, the flying fortresses of Tripura and the wondrous assembly hall of the Pandavas, and was the father of Mandodari, queen of Ravana.
nodes.story: When Agni devoured the Khandava forest, guarded by Krishna and Arjuna, the Danava Maya fled from the flames. Agni pursued him and Krishna raised his discus, but Maya cried out to Arjuna for protection, and Arjuna promised him his life. In gratitude Maya offered to build something for the Pandavas, and at Krishna's suggestion he raised the Maya Sabha at Indraprastha for Yudhishthira. Its crystal floors looked like pools and its pools looked like floors, and its jewelled halls rivalled the courts of the gods. Maya also brought Bhima a mighty mace and Arjuna the conch Devadatta. Later, when Duryodhana toured the hall, he mistook water for floor and fell in, and the laughter that followed deepened the resentment that led to the game of dice.
nodes.abode: Tripura; the golden cave of the Riksha-bila; Atala (Bhagavata)
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Kishkindha Kanda (Riksha-bila and Hema)
Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Khandava) and Sabha Parva 1-3
variations: In the Kishkindha Kanda he builds a golden forest-city for the apsara Hema and is killed by Indra's vajra; in the Mahabharata and Puranas he lives on.
In the Uttara Kanda he gives his daughter Mandodari to Ravana; his sons Mayavi and Dundubhi fight Vali.
Several Puranas say Shiva spared Maya when Tripura burned because of his devotion.
Indian astronomical tradition credits Maya with receiving the Surya Siddhanta from the Sun.

nodes.name: Rahu (Svarbhanu)
nodes.description: The shadow planet of eclipses, the immortal severed head of the asura Svarbhanu. In the Rig Veda Svarbhanu pierces the sun with darkness; in the epics he steals a sip of amrita at the churning of the ocean and is beheaded by Vishnu, and he becomes one of the Navagraha, the ascending node of the Moon.
nodes.story: When Vishnu, as the enchantress Mohini, served the nectar of immortality to the devas after the churning of the ocean, the asura Svarbhanu slipped into the line disguised as a god and sat between the Sun and the Moon. He had just begun to drink when Surya and Chandra recognised him and cried out. Vishnu's discus flashed and severed his head before the amrita could pass his throat. But the head had already tasted immortality: it rose into the sky as Rahu, while the headless body became Ketu. Ever since, Rahu has pursued the Sun and Moon to take revenge. When he catches and swallows one of them, the world sees an eclipse, but the light soon escapes through his severed neck. Long before, the Rig Veda had sung of Svarbhanu piercing the sun with darkness until Atri restored it.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 17 (churning of the ocean)
Vishnu Purana 2.12 (chariots of Rahu and Ketu)
variations: The Bhagavata Purana (6.18) makes Rahu the son of the Danava Viprachitti and Simhika, whence the name Saimhikeya; its list of Danu's sons (6.6) also includes Svarbhanu.
In the Rig Veda Svarbhanu is an eclipsing asura without the beheading story, which first appears in the Mahabharata.
Some Puranas say Brahma or Vishnu granted Rahu and Ketu a place among the planets and a share of offerings.
In Jyotisha Rahu is the north (ascending) lunar node.

nodes.name: Ketu
nodes.description: The shadow planet formed from the headless body of the asura Svarbhanu, whose head became Rahu. One of the Navagraha, Ketu is the descending node of the Moon, linked with eclipses, comets, detachment and liberation (moksha) in Jyotisha.
nodes.story: When Vishnu's discus beheaded Svarbhanu at the distribution of the amrita, the head and body did not die, for both had been touched by the nectar. The head rose as Rahu; the body, writhing and headless, became Ketu. Unable to rejoin, the two were placed in the sky as shadowy planets exactly opposite one another, the points where the paths of the Sun and Moon cross, and together they are held responsible for eclipses. Ketu's lack of a head became a symbol: in astrological lore he is the planet of renunciation and inner insight, without worldly ambition, and the bringer of sudden changes and spiritual release. His name also means banner or bright sign, and trailing comets, dhumaketu or smoke-bannered, were counted among his many forms.
variations: In early texts ketu means a comet or bright sign; its role as the headless body of Svarbhanu and as the ninth graha develops in Puranic and astrological texts.
Some Puranas speak of many Ketus (comets) rather than a single graha.
In Jyotisha Ketu is the south (descending) lunar node, often linked with Ganesha as presiding deity.

nodes.name: Narakasura
nodes.description: The asura king of Pragjyotisha (associated with ancient Assam), son of the Earth goddess Bhudevi, fathered in many accounts by Vishnu as Varaha. He stole the earrings of Aditi and imprisoned thousands of princesses until Krishna, with Satyabhama, slew him; his death is celebrated as Naraka Chaturdashi on the eve of Diwali.
nodes.story: Naraka, son of the Earth, grew arrogant in his impregnable city of Pragjyotisha. He seized the umbrella of Varuna and the jewelled earrings of Aditi, mother of the gods, and carried off sixteen thousand maidens to his palace. Indra went to Dvaraka to plead for help, and Krishna rode out on Garuda with Satyabhama beside him. He smashed the mountain forts and the fields of nooses, slew the five-headed Mura who guarded the city, and destroyed Naraka's army. When Naraka hurled his spear, Krishna cut off his head with the discus. Bhudevi herself then came forward, returned Aditi's earrings and asked Krishna to protect Naraka's son Bhagadatta. Krishna freed the captive women and, to spare them from shame, accepted them all as his wives.
sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva and Udyoga Parva (references to Krishna slaying Naraka)
variations: The Kalika Purana makes him the son of Varaha and Bhudevi, raised by King Janaka, installed as guardian of the goddess Kamakhya, and later cursed by Vasishtha after turning impious.
In many South Indian and Deepavali tellings Satyabhama, as an incarnation of Bhudevi, delivers the fatal blow, since he could be killed only by his mother.
The number of captive women is given as sixteen thousand or sixteen thousand one hundred.
At his request, his death day is observed as Naraka Chaturdashi with lamps and ritual baths.

nodes.name: Kalanemi
nodes.description: A mighty Danava who led the asuras in the Tarakamaya war against the gods and was slain by Vishnu; the Harivamsha and Bhagavata say he was reborn as Kamsa. A different Kalanemi, a rakshasa uncle of Ravana, appears in later Ramayana traditions trying to stop Hanuman.
nodes.story: In the great war over Tara, wife of Brihaspati, the Danava Kalanemi rose against the devas like a mountain of darkness. The Harivamsha describes how he scattered the gods and took over the functions of the guardians of the world, claiming the sacrificial offerings for himself. The gods fled to Vishnu, who came mounted on Garuda. Kalanemi hurled his weapons at him, but Vishnu cut off the Danava's head with the Sudarshana discus. In another age, the Bhagavata and Harivamsha say, this same Kalanemi was born as Kamsa, the tyrant of Mathura, once again to be slain by Vishnu, now as Krishna. Later Ramayana retellings add a rakshasa Kalanemi who, disguised as a hermit, tried to delay Hanuman on his journey to the healing herb, and was killed by him.
variations: The Danava of the Harivamsha and the rakshasa who opposes Hanuman are usually regarded as different beings sharing a name.
The Vishnu Purana and Harivamsha say the six sons of Devaki killed by Kamsa had been sons of Kalanemi in an earlier birth.
The rakshasa Kalanemi is absent from Valmiki's Ramayana.

nodes.name: Vatapi
nodes.description: A Daitya who could take the form of a ram or goat and be cooked and eaten, then burst alive out of the eater's belly at his brother Ilvala's call. He met his end when the sage Agastya ate him and digested him completely.
nodes.story: Ilvala and Vatapi hated brahmins and devised a cruel trick. Ilvala would invite a brahmin guest to a feast and serve him a meal of meat, which was Vatapi transformed into a ram. When the guest had eaten, Ilvala would call out his brother's name, and Vatapi would tear his way out of the guest's belly, killing him. Many brahmins died this way, until the sage Agastya came to their house. He ate the whole dish with calm contentment. Ilvala called, 'Vatapi, come out!', but nothing happened. Agastya smiled, patted his stomach and said that Vatapi had already been digested; the words 'Vatapi, be digested' became a proverb. The Chalukya capital Vatapi, modern Badami, bears his name.
variations: The Bhagavata makes Vatapi and Ilvala sons of Hlada, brother of Prahlada, and his wife Dhamani.
In the Mahabharata Agastya comes to Ilvala seeking wealth to satisfy Lopamudra; in the Ramayana the tale is told as one of Agastya's great deeds for the forest-dwelling sages.

nodes.name: Ilvala
nodes.description: A Daitya king, brother of Vatapi, who used his brother's shape-shifting to murder brahmin guests at feasts. The Ramayana says the sage Agastya burned him with a glance after digesting Vatapi; the Mahabharata says he gave Agastya great wealth instead.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata explains Ilvala's hatred: he once asked a brahmin to give him a son equal to Indra, and when the brahmin refused, he vowed revenge on all brahmins. When Agastya needed wealth to provide the ornaments his bride Lopamudra asked for, he went with three kings to Ilvala, who was famed for his riches. Ilvala welcomed them with his usual feast of Vatapi, but the sage ate it all and digested it. Stunned and afraid, Ilvala asked what they wanted, and Agastya asked for wealth. Ilvala gave each king a fortune in cows and gold, and gave Agastya even more, with a golden chariot drawn by two swift horses. In the Ramayana, however, when Ilvala rushed at the sage in rage, Agastya reduced him to ashes with the fire of his gaze.
variations: Ramayana: Agastya burns Ilvala to death; Mahabharata: Ilvala survives and pays Agastya tribute.
The Bhagavata makes him a grandson of Hiranyakashipu through Hlada.

nodes.name: Sunda
nodes.description: An asura of Hiranyakashipu's line, son of Nikumbha, who with his inseparable brother Upasunda won from Brahma a boon that nothing but each other could kill them. The gods had the apsara Tilottama created to set them against each other, and the brothers destroyed one another.
nodes.story: Sunda and Upasunda shared everything: one kingdom, one bed, one meal, one will. They performed such austerities on the Vindhya mountains that Brahma granted them mastery of every art and freedom from death at the hands of any being except each other. Secure in this boon, they conquered the three worlds, drove the gods from heaven and harassed the sages. Brahma then asked Vishvakarma to create a woman from the finest particle of every beautiful thing in creation; she was named Tilottama. She appeared, gathering flowers, where the brothers were drinking and feasting on the Vindhya slopes. Each seized one of her hands and claimed her as his wife. Their unbroken love turned to fury; they grabbed their maces and struck each other dead. Tilottama returned to Brahma, and the worlds were at peace.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 201-204 (Sunda and Upasunda episode)
variations: Narada tells the story to the Pandavas so that they will agree on a rule for sharing Draupadi and avoid quarrelling over her.
A different Sunda appears in the Ramayana as the husband of the yakshini Tataka and father of Maricha.

nodes.name: Upasunda
nodes.description: The younger brother of Sunda, son of the asura Nikumbha in Hiranyakashipu's line. He shared a boon of near-invincibility with his brother, and the two killed each other in a quarrel over the apsara Tilottama.
nodes.story: When the Pandavas married Draupadi together, the sage Narada came to them with a warning drawn from the tale of Upasunda and his elder brother Sunda. The two asura brothers had never been apart and never disagreed. Their austerities won them Brahma's promise that only they could kill each other, which seemed a harmless condition for brothers so united. After they had overrun heaven and earth, the gods sent Tilottama, the most beautiful woman ever fashioned. The moment she walked into their garden, Sunda declared her his wife, and so an elder sister-in-law to Upasunda; Upasunda declared her his own, and so a younger brother's wife to Sunda. Soon they were fighting. Blinded by desire, the inseparable pair beat each other to death with maces. Hearing this, the Pandavas agreed that whoever intruded on a brother alone with Draupadi would go into exile for twelve years.
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva 201-204 (Sunda and Upasunda episode)
variations: The story is a teaching tale within the Mahabharata; Upasunda is not significant outside it.

nodes.name: Kali (spirit of the Kali Yuga)
nodes.description: Kali (with a short 'a', distinct from the goddess Kali) is the personification of the Kali Yuga, the dark age of strife, and of the losing throw of the dice. He possesses King Nala in the Mahabharata, is restrained by King Parikshit in the Bhagavata, and is destined to be destroyed by Kalki at the end of the age.
nodes.story: Kali arrived too late for Damayanti's svayamvara and learned, to his fury, that she had chosen the mortal Nala over the gods themselves. He vowed to ruin Nala and waited twelve years for a lapse in the king's purity. When Nala once performed his evening rites without washing his feet properly, Kali entered him. Possessed, Nala gambled away his kingdom to his brother Pushkara and wandered in the forest, even abandoning Damayanti as she slept. Damayanti's grief-stricken curse and the venom of the serpent Karkotaka, who bit Nala, tormented the spirit within him. At last, when Nala learned the secret of dice from King Rituparna, Kali was forced out, trembling, and took refuge in a vibhitaka tree. Kali begged forgiveness and promised that those who recite Nala's story would be free from his influence.
nodes.abode: Places of gambling, drinking, lust, slaughter and gold (Bhagavata); the vibhitaka tree (Mahabharata)
sources: Mahabharata, Adi Parva (Duryodhana as a portion of Kali)
variations: In the Bhagavata Purana Parikshit finds Kali beating the bull of Dharma, raises his sword, but spares him when he surrenders and assigns him places to dwell.
The Mahabharata says Duryodhana was born from a portion of Kali.
The Kalki Purana gives Kali a genealogy descended from Adharma and describes his final defeat by Kalki.
He must not be confused with the goddess Kali (Kālī), with whom he has no connection.

nodes.name: Madhu
nodes.description: One of the twin primordial asuras, Madhu and Kaitabha, who sprang from the ear-wax of Vishnu as he slept on the cosmic ocean and threatened Brahma. Vishnu slew them, earning the name Madhusudana, 'slayer of Madhu'.
nodes.story: At the end of a cosmic age, Vishnu slept on the serpent Shesha upon the endless waters, and from the wax of his ears two terrible asuras were born, Madhu and Kaitabha. Seeing Brahma seated on the lotus that rose from Vishnu's navel, they rushed to kill him. Brahma, terrified, sang praises to Yoganidra, the Great Goddess of sleep who held Vishnu's eyes closed. She withdrew from him, and Vishnu awoke and fought the brothers with his bare arms for five thousand years. Bewildered by the Goddess, the proud asuras offered to grant him a boon; Vishnu asked only that they die by his hand. Seeing water everywhere, they agreed on condition that he kill them where the earth was not flooded. Vishnu laid them on his thighs and struck off their heads with his discus.
variations: In the Narayaniya of the Shanti Parva Madhu and Kaitabha steal the Vedas from Brahma, and Vishnu, having recovered them in the horse-headed form of Hayagriva, slays the pair.
The Devi Bhagavata says they had won from the Goddess the boon of dying only when they chose.
The earth is called Medini because it was formed from their fat or marrow (Devi Bhagavata and other Puranas).
The Ramayana's Uttara Kanda has a different Madhu, a Danava father of Lavana, who is slain by Shatrughna.

nodes.name: Kaitabha
nodes.description: Twin of Madhu, the second of the primordial asuras born from the ear-wax of the sleeping Vishnu. With his brother he attacked Brahma and was slain by Vishnu once the goddess Yoganidra released him from sleep; Vishnu is thus called Kaitabhajit.
nodes.story: The Narayaniya of the Mahabharata tells another version of the twins' career. When Brahma was creating the worlds from the lotus of Vishnu's navel, the four Vedas lay before him in embodied form. Madhu and Kaitabha, born from two drops of water on the lotus, seized the Vedas and dived with them into the depths of Rasatala, leaving Brahma blind to the knowledge he needed to create. Grieving, Brahma prayed to Vishnu, who took the horse-headed form of Hayagriva. Chanting the Sama Veda in a deep voice, he descended into the netherworld, recovered the Vedas and returned them to Brahma. When the asuras came back and found them gone, they searched for the thief and challenged Vishnu, who slew them both, and Brahma could resume creation.
variations: In the Devi Mahatmya they arise from Vishnu's ear-wax; in the Narayaniya from drops of water on the lotus.
The Mahabharata's Vana Parva makes the asura Dhundhu, slain by King Kuvalashva (Dhundhumara), the son of Madhu and Kaitabha.

edges.label: Madhu attacked Brahma seated on the lotus
The Goddess as Yoganidra and Mahamaya woke Vishnu and bewildered Madhu (Devi Mahatmya 1)
Vishnu as Hayagriva recovered the Vedas stolen by Madhu and slew him (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva)
edges.variation: Narayaniya version; other texts credit Vishnu in his sleeping form

edges.label: The Goddess granted Madhu the boon of dying only when he chose (Devi Bhagavata 1)
edges.variation: Devi Bhagavata only

edges.label: Vishnu slew Kaitabha on his thighs with the discus (Devi Mahatmya 1)
Kaitabha sprang from the ear-wax of the sleeping Vishnu (Devi Mahatmya 1)
edges.variation: In the Narayaniya they arise from drops of water on the lotus
